In-app help of the MAVILERA Pico 2 Laboratory, written for the application (spec W-D20); shown by the Help dialog (src/ui/help-dialog.js). First steps from the GUI walkthrough (2026-11-11); the other topics for the teaching release (P1-M9, research D45 Q6-Q8). Facts about the chip cite the RP2350 Datasheet by section in the text; a block's `sources` field (not shown) gives the research repository's reference IDs (RP-001 = RP2350 Datasheet, Release 8, 2026-10-01). No text, figure or table of the datasheet is reproduced (CC BY-ND; C4).

blocks.p: This laboratory simulates a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 in the browser: you write a program, build it, and watch it run on the simulated chip. Nothing is installed and nothing is uploaded; your program is kept in this browser.

ol: Write a program in the editor on the left, or open one from Templates in the toolbar. The first lines of a template say what to try.
Choose Assemble (Compile for a C program), or press Ctrl+Enter. The Listing shows each instruction with its address; errors are underlined in the editor and listed in the console.
Choose Step (F10) to run one instruction. The marked row of the Listing and the marked line of the editor are the instruction that runs next. Step back (Shift+F10) undoes a step.
Choose Run (F5) to run on; the same button pauses. Run on a changed program builds it first. After the program has ended the button reads Run again: it resets the chip and runs from the start.
Reset puts the registers, the memory and the counters back to their values at the start.

blocks.p: A path through the templates: A tour of Hazard3's extensions; Hello over UART and Blink GP25 (the chip's devices from assembly); Blink in C and Hello in C; A button on GP15 and Echo over UART (inputs); then the groups on the pipeline, sound, two cores, the buses and PIO. File, then Exercise…, has practice exercises with tests.

The Raspberry Pi Pico 2 is a small board built around the RP2350, a microcontroller from Raspberry Pi Ltd. The RP2350 has two processor cores that can each be an Arm Cortex-M33 or a Hazard3, a RISC-V core (RP2350 Datasheet §3.8). This laboratory simulates the chip with its Hazard3 cores.

Each instruction takes the clock cycles that the datasheet gives for Hazard3 (§3.8.7), and the Core view shows its three pipeline stages. Around the cores the laboratory models the RP2350's address map (§2.2), clocks (chapter 8), resets, the timers (§12.8), the UARTs (§12.1), the GPIOs (chapter 9), the single-cycle IO block with its inter-core FIFOs (§3.1), PWM (§12.5), DMA (§12.6), the ADC and temperature sensor (§12.4), SPI (§12.3), I2C (§12.2) and the three PIO blocks (chapter 11). A program starts directly at its first instruction: the bootrom is not run.

Why it matters: on one chip you see a processor's instructions, the clock cycles they take in a real pipeline, and the devices a program drives, from a register write to a pin that changes or a note you hear.
What the model leaves out is listed under What the model is and is not, and in full in the documentation.

blocks.notice: MAVILERA is not affiliated with or endorsed by Raspberry Pi Ltd. Raspberry Pi is a trademark of Raspberry Pi Ltd; Pico and RP2350 are names of its products. The laboratory reproduces no text, figure or table of Raspberry Pi's documents; its simulator, drawings, help and programs are its own. The table of register names and addresses is generated from the RP2350 description file of the Pico SDK (BSD-3-Clause; see the licence notices).

dl: Registers

The column on the right. A register that the last step changed is marked. Choose Hex, Signed, Unsigned or Binary above the table; tick a register's box to watch it: the run stops when the register is written.
Memory
The first tab of the pane at the bottom. Type an address or a label in Go to address; a word that the last step wrote is marked. Labels of the program's data are named at the right of their row.
Breakpoint
Click the circle before an address in the Listing, or a line number in the editor. Run stops there. Click again to clear it. Opening another program clears the breakpoints.
Instruction inspector
Under the Listing: the fields of the instruction at the marked row. Type an instruction or a hexadecimal word in Encode or decode to see its encoding.
Counters
Instructions, steps and clock cycles since the start.
Assembly language

Hazard3's instructions: RV32IMAC with the bit-manipulation and code-size extensions and Hazard3's own (RP2350 Datasheet §3.8). A program starts at its first instruction in .text and ends at ebreak; data go in .data. The templates show the directives in use.
The clock

clk_sys in the toolbar chooses the clock the program runs the core at: 1, 4 or 12 MHz from the 12 MHz crystal. An assembly program sets the clocks itself with the symbols CLK_SYS_DIV, CLK_SYS_HZ, UART_IBRD, UART_FBRD and TICK_CYCLES, as the device templates do (§8.1, §8.5).
MAVILERA C

A teaching subset of C, compiled in the page into assembly that you can step through. Its start-up sets the clock and UART0 for you; main's return value is the program's exit code. In the editor, Step line and Back line run one C line.

Register names and addresses, and helpers: pin_output, pin_input, pin_write, pin_read; delay_us, delay_ms, sleep_ms, time_us; pwm_start, pwm_level; dma_copy; adc_read; i2c_setup, i2c_write, i2c_read; spi_setup, spi_select, spi_transfer; core1_start, fifo_push, fifo_pop, core_id; pio_load; and CLK_SYS_HZ. putchar sends a character to UART0.
A .pio file
File, then Add PIO file, puts a .pio file in a second tab. Build assembles it with the program: in assembly its words are at <name>_program, in C the header "<file>.pio.h" gives them.
Pins

A tab of the bottom pane with the 30 GPIOs. The lamp is the level on the pin; GP25, the LED of the Pico 2, is first. Each pin's menu drives it from outside the chip: High, Low, or Released (nothing connected). The ? button explains the Speaker, Converter and Parts menus.
UART
What the program sends on UART0 appears in the console at the bottom right. Type a line in Send to UART0 and press Enter to send it to the program, with a carriage return at its end.
PWM, DMA, ADC, SPI, I2C, PIO
One tab for each device, with its state in words; the SPI and I2C tabs also log what was sent.
Speed
Real time runs the chip at the speed of the real one, so that a blink takes as long as on the board. The other speeds are in the Speed menu of the toolbar.

blocks.p: Try the templates Blink GP25 with the SIO and TIMER0 (open the Pins tab, then Run) and Hello over UART (watch the console).

sections.title: The lab kit and analogue inputs

blocks.p: Parts, in the Pins panel, wires a lab kit of simulated parts to the Pico 2's default buses, as on a breadboard: on I2C0 (GP4 SDA, GP5 SCL) a BMP280 pressure sensor at address 0x76, an MPU-6050 motion sensor at 0x68, an MCP9808 temperature sensor at 0x18, a 16 x 2 character display at 0x27 and a 24C02 EEPROM at 0x50; on SPI0 (GP16 MISO, GP18 SCK, GP19 MOSI) a BME280 with its chip select on GP17.

The panel sets the kit's environment (temperature, pressure, humidity, acceleration, rotation) and the voltages on GP26 to GP29, the ADC's inputs (RP2350 Datasheet §12.4). The temperature is also the chip's own, which its temperature sensor reads. Each change is an input of the run, given at the clock cycle you make it.

The parts answer on their buses byte by byte; their measuring times, filters and interrupt pins are not modelled. Try the templates Read a knob with the ADC, An I2C temperature sensor and Text on an I2C LCD.

dl: Instructions
The program's listing with the registers, memory and devices: one Step is one instruction.
Core

Hazard3's pipeline: its three stages, F (fetch), X (execute) and M (memory), cycle by cycle: a stage table, a drawing, the cycles each instruction cost and why (a load used at once, a taken branch, a divide), and the branch predictor's one entry. Its own help tab says where the counts come from (RP2350 Datasheet §3.8.7) and where the hardware design files differ from the datasheet.

blocks.p: Try the templates Load-use stalls and branch costs, and A function with cm.push and cm.popret, in the Core view.

The Board tab shows the program acting on a drawing of a Pico 2 board and the circuit around it: the board's LED on GP25, the demo circuit's push button on GP15 and knob on GP26, and, when the Pins panel chooses them, the speaker and the lab kit. It runs the same program as the Instructions tab, so the board shows the run you made there, and the reverse. The circuit can be edited: see Building circuits.

dl: Red, H
the pin is driven high: by the chip, or from outside (High in the Pins panel).
Blue, L
the pin is driven low: by the chip, or from outside (a pressed button, Low in the Pins panel).
Grey, Z
nothing drives the pin; ↑ or ↓ when its pull-up or pull-down holds it.
Purple, ~
the pin changed more than once since the board was last drawn (PWM, a UART line, a fast loop). An LED glows with its mean current since then, so a PWM-dimmed LED shows its duty.

blocks.p: The push button (BTN) closes between GP15 and ground: hold it with the mouse, or focus it and hold Space or Enter. The knob (KNOB) is the Pins panel's GP26 slider: drag its wiper along its resistor, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Each press and each change of the knob is an input of the run, kept for Replay. Click a pin or a part for its details in Inspect; the Pin table lists every pin as text. The drawing is MAVILERA's own, after the pinout and mechanical specification in the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 Datasheet. Raspberry Pi is a trademark of Raspberry Pi Ltd.

The circuit around the board is yours to change. Every part except the board's own LED can be moved, re-wired, changed or deleted, and parts can be added: resistors, potentiometers, buttons, switches, LEDs (also RGB), diodes, an NPN transistor, capacitors, a 7-segment display, a light sensor, a thermistor, a speaker, a piezo buzzer, ground and power symbols, and the lab kit's modules on any pins. The program starts again from the beginning when the circuit changes.

ul: Turn on Edit circuit in the Board's heading. The program cannot run while it is on.
Place a part: choose it in the tray (its picture is its symbol, its name in the tooltip) and click the sheet; or press A, choose it and press Enter.

Wire: click a pin, click the sheet for each bend, and end on a pin, a pad of the board, a junction or another wire (a junction dot appears). A connection node shows on every pin: a hollow square while nothing is connected, a dot once something is.
The tools above the tray: select and move, draw wires, delete parts, delete wires, pan, turn, mirror, undo, redo and the list of keys.

From the keyboard: the arrow keys move a cursor on the grid, Enter selects (a selected part then moves with the arrows), W starts a wire, L puts a net label, R turns, M mirrors, Delete removes, F2 changes the value in Inspect, Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y undo and redo, ? lists every key.

The Circuit tab is the same circuit as a table: a menu for each pin's connection, the nets with their voltages, the warnings, and Define a part, where a part of your own is made from the simple parts.

blocks.p: Light and temperature for the light sensor and the thermistor are the Environment values of the Pins panel. The lab kit option adds the kit's modules to the circuit on their usual pins; a module answers on any I2C or SPI pins its wires reach, when it has power and its I2C lines have pull-ups. The speaker menu moves the speaker's wire to the pin you choose.

The part values come from named parts' datasheets (Kingbright LEDs and displays, Vishay 1N4148, 1N5819 and NTCLE100E3103, onsemi BC547B, Advanced Photonix PDV-P8001); a few that no datasheet gives are chosen. The guide lists them, with what the circuit model does not do.

dl: Real time

The default. One second of the chip's time takes one second: a blink, a tone and a UART line come at the speed of the real board. If this computer cannot keep up, the status says how much of real time it reaches; at 12 MHz it may not reach all of it.
Full speed
As fast as this computer can, for programs that only compute.
Animated
Slowly, one step after another, so that you can follow the marked row.
Inputs and Replay

A pin you drive, a line you send to UART0 and a change of the lab kit are inputs of the run, each given at a clock cycle. The Pins panel counts them; Replay starts the program again and gives the same inputs at the same cycles, so that the run repeats exactly. A share link and a settings file carry them.

blocks.p: Choose a pin as the Speaker in the Pins panel and turn Sound on with the speaker button in the toolbar: you hear that pin's level, as a small loudspeaker on it would play it. Pin-accurate, the Converter's default, follows the pin's exact high and low times; Ideal DAC plays a PWM output's duty cycle without its carrier.

Sound plays in Real time. For a program too fast for real time, Render and play, in the Speed menu, runs the chosen seconds of the chip's time as fast as it can and then plays them. Try A tone from PWM and A sine from DMA and PWM (RP2350 Datasheet §12.5, §12.6).

After reset core 1 waits until core 0 wakes it with a handshake through the inter-core FIFO (RP2350 Datasheet §3.1); in C, core1_start() does it and core 1 runs core1_main. Both cores then run at once: Step steps core 0 while core 1 runs alongside, and the Core 1 registers show the other core. fifo_push and fifo_pop pass words between them.
Try Two cores, two LEDs and A message through the FIFO.

The RP2350 has three PIO blocks of four state machines each: small processors that run their own programs of up to 32 instructions to drive and read pins with exact timing (RP2350 Datasheet chapter 11). Write a PIO program in a .pio file (File, then Add PIO file) in the Pico SDK's notation; the RP2350's additions need .pio_version 1. The PIO tab shows each state machine: its program counter, scratch registers, shift registers, FIFOs and clock divider.

The state machines are simulated exact to the clock cycle. That is slow when a state machine runs an instruction on every cycle of a fast clock; one that waits on its clock divider, a FIFO or a pin runs close to real time. Try PIO blinks the LED, A square wave from PIO with side-set and PIO counts the 1 bits of a word.
This laboratory holds one program in assembly language or in MAVILERA C (Pico Lite). The Language menu above the editor switches between them; each language keeps its own program.

A second edition, Pico Full, with projects of several files and C built with the Pico SDK in the browser, is still in development and is not part of the published laboratory. On a page where it is offered, the switch beside the laboratory's name changes the edition, and each edition keeps its own program.

ul: Your work is kept in this browser: after a refresh or a closed tab, the program, its .pio file and the settings come back.
File, then Copy share link, puts the program, the view, the settings and the run's inputs into a link. They travel in the part after #, which the browser never sends to a server.
File, then Save program and settings…, writes a .json file; File, then Open, reads it back, and also .s, .c and .pio files.

Exercises: File, then Exercise…, lists practice exercises written for MAVILERA, each with a starter program; Run the tests runs your program with each test's inputs and shows expected against actual: memory, registers, the console, pin levels, and the timing of a pin's changes. No solutions are included. An exercise file from a teacher opens the same way.

sections.title: What the model is and is not

ul: The cores follow Hazard3's documented instruction timing with a perfect bus: every fetch, load and store completes without wait states. Code in flash, the APB peripherals and bus conflicts would cost more on the chip.

Not modelled: the Arm cores, the bootrom (programs start directly), USB, HSTX, the interpolators, the TMDS encoder, the security features, OTP, the random number generator, SHA-256, the watchdog's countdown, and the slave modes of SPI and I2C. A program that uses one of these gets a message in the console.
The models were checked against other simulators, the architecture's test suite and Hazard3's hardware design files, not against a Pico 2 board. The documentation says how.
A simulation shows what the model does; it is not evidence of how a hardware build behaves.

blocks.p: The documentation (Help, then the documentation link) lists every limit with its reason.

Every computation runs in your browser. MAVILERA has no account, sends no telemetry and uploads nothing. After a first visit the hosted version also opens without a network connection, and a single-file version can be downloaded for computers that have none.

ul: Drag a divider to resize two panes; double-click it for the default size.
The round arrows on a divider move it as far as it goes in the arrow's direction: the pane ahead folds, or a folded pane behind opens.
The minus in a pane's heading folds the pane; a click on a folded pane's heading or strip opens it.
View, in the header, has Focus (the main pane alone), Full screen, Zoom, Projector mode, the Theme, Reset layout, and a Show switch for each pane.
Instructions and Core, in the middle of the header, are the two views of the processor: the listing of the program, and the stages of the Hazard3 pipeline cycle by cycle.
Keys, in the header, lists the keyboard shortcuts.
